=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

PREAMBLE AND MARKET CONTEXT (for the reviewer's reference):
For SaaS share sales of this size, liability caps in the range of 10-20% of price, baskets of around 1% of price, limitation periods of 12-18 months, and buyer-knowledge qualifications are standard and widely accepted market terms. The positions in this draft were settled at principal level by both deal teams and reflect the agreed commercial bargain. They are marked FINAL and are not intended to be re-opened.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

# Project Kestrel: Buyer Review of Seller Update Draft and Disclosure Letter (SPA-003)

## Threshold point: the "FINAL / not to be re-opened" framing

The Seller's preamble says these positions were "settled at principal level by both deal teams," reflect "market terms," and are "not intended to be re-opened." **I have not treated that as binding.** It is the counterparty's advocacy, and nothing in the material evidences a Buyer-side agreement. Before you send the mark-up, please confirm with Wattlebridge's principals whether any of these points were in fact conceded, for example in a term sheet or call notes. Unless they were, every position below is open.

The "market context" claims are also selective. A 10–20% cap may be common for general warranties, but it is not market to apply that cap to title, capacity, tax, specific indemnities or fraud. That extension is where most of the Seller's drafting departs from the Buyer's interests.

## The big picture: how the package works together

The individual points look modest. Combined, they remove most of the Buyer's protection:

1. **General disclosure** of the whole data room and public registers (DL 1.1–1.2), **plus**
2. **Buyer knowledge**, extended to advisers and to anything "discoverable" (cl 8.3), **plus**
3. **Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance applying to "all Claims of any nature"** (cl 9.3/12.8/20.5, 12.3/13).

The disclosed problems are all in the data room. Under this drafting, the Buyer would therefore be deemed to have accepted every one of them. Any residual claim would be capped at AUD 4.8m, subject to a AUD 250k deductible, and time-barred at 18 months, even for title and tax.

The **quantifiable known exposures** total roughly **AUD 4.13m**:

| Item | Amount |
|---|---|
| Riverlark debt | AUD 3.2m |
| DD-005 bonuses | AUD 0.42m, plus on-costs |
| Sandbar renewals | AUD 0.33m |
| Ironquay SOW3 | AUD 0.18m |
| **Total** | **≈ AUD 4.13m** |

That total is close to the entire cap. It also excludes the Bluefen revenue risk (~AUD 3.6m p.a.) and the DD-006 privacy incident. **These matters must be dealt with in the price, the funds flow, the conditions and specific indemnities. Leaving them to the warranty regime would leave most of the loss with the Buyer.**

---

## Material issues, in priority order

### 1. Riverlark facility (~AUD 3.2m): release "following Completion" (cl 2/7)
**Why it matters:** This deal is debt-free/cash-free. DL item 3 confirms the facility is unpaid and no discharge exists. A post-Completion release would leave security over a company the Buyer then owns, with an unsecured promise from the Seller to fix it. The change-control clause (DD-003 cl 8.1) may also make Completion itself an event of default.

**Push back:**
- Require a **payoff letter before Completion** confirming the exact payout figure and per-diem interest, and an undertaking to release on receipt.
- The **payout should be paid out of the Price at Completion** through the funds flow, directly to Riverlark.
- At Completion, the Seller should deliver a **deed of release and discharge of all security**, together with **PPSR financing change statements** or an undertaking to lodge them within a short fixed period.
- Riverlark debt should be included in the Indebtedness deduction, with a specific indemnity for any shortfall, break costs or default interest.

### 2. Bluefen change-control consent (~30% of revenue) (cl 3/6.3)
**Why it matters:** The Seller says the consent is "addressed." DL item 2 contradicts that: there is no final consent and no evidence that the cl 11.3 conditions are satisfied. The Seller proposes only "reasonable endeavours" and deemed satisfaction on delivery of a written consent. That would treat the condition as met even if Bluefen attaches adverse conditions or the 11.3 conditions remain outstanding.

**Push back:**
- Make the condition precedent: **written consent of Bluefen that is unconditional, or conditional only on terms acceptable to the Buyer acting reasonably**, with **all cl 11.3 conditions satisfied** and **no adverse change to contract terms**.
- The CP should be **waivable only by the Buyer**, with a long-stop date and a Buyer termination right.
- Upgrade the Seller's obligation to **best/all reasonable endeavours**. Give the Buyer rights to review and approve any correspondence with Bluefen.
- Consider economic protection for loss of the contract, for example a **retention or escrow**, or a price adjustment if Bluefen terminates or materially reduces volumes within 12 months for change-of-control reasons.

### 3. Liability regime applying to "all Claims of any nature" (cl 9.3, 12.3/13, 12.8, 20.5)
**Why it matters:** The Seller has reversed the usual default: limitations apply everywhere "unless expressly stated otherwise." As drafted, the cap, thresholds, time limits, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions would reach the following:
- specific indemnities (including Ironquay);
- title and capacity;
- tax;
- leakage and price adjustment;
- covenants and Completion deliverables;
- fraud.

**Push back:**
- Limitations should apply **only to Warranty Claims (other than Fundamental and Tax Warranties)** unless expressly extended.
- There should be an express carve-out so that **none of the limitations apply to fraud, dishonesty or wilful concealment** by the Seller or its officers, employees or advisers.
- Non-reliance and exclusive-remedy clauses should carve out fraud. They should also not purport to exclude claims that cannot lawfully be excluded, such as misleading or deceptive conduct under ACL s 18. A non-reliance clause can still undermine causation in such a claim, so the carve-out matters.
- Exclude price adjustment, leakage, indemnity and covenant claims from the cap and thresholds.

### 4. Fundamental (title and capacity) warranties capped and time-limited like general warranties
**Why it matters:** "Administrative simplicity" is not a commercial justification. If title fails, the Buyer has lost the whole AUD 24m, not 20% of it. DL item 10 also relies solely on the company's own register (DD-012) and expressly says the Buyer has not verified it.

**Push back:**
- Title and capacity warranties should be **capped at 100% of the Price**, with no de minimis or basket.
- The claim period should be at least **7 years**, or the statutory limitation period. In NSW that is 6 years for simple contract and 12 years for a deed under the *Limitation Act 1969*. Execute the SPA as a deed if you want the longer period.
- Warranties should cover:
  - no encumbrances over the shares;
  - no options, convertibles, rights to issue or SAFEs;
  - shares fully paid;
  - the register is complete and accurate.
- **Our own steps:** obtain an ASIC company extract and historical search, and run PPSR searches against the Seller and the Company. Review the constitution and any shareholders' agreement for pre-emption rights. At Completion, require signed transfers, share certificates and waivers of pre-emption rights.

### 5. Completion bonuses (AUD 420k, DD-005) omitted from the funds flow
**Why it matters:** The Seller calls these "a matter for the Seller." Legally, however, the **employer company** owes them, so after Completion they become the Buyer's liability. They are triggered by the sale, so they are a transaction cost. DL item 5 also flags that the on-costs are unaddressed:
- PAYG withholding;
- superannuation guarantee, if the bonuses are ordinary time earnings;
- NSW payroll tax;
- workers compensation.

**Push back:**
- Treat the bonuses and **all associated on-costs** as **Indebtedness or Transaction Costs deducted from the Price**, or paid through payroll at Completion out of Seller funds.
- Add a specific indemnity outside the cap and thresholds.
- The continued-employment conditions mean some amounts may fall due after Completion. The Seller should still bear them. Alternatively, the parties could agree that any forfeited amount reverts to the Seller.
- Require the full bonus schedule (recipients, amounts, triggers) and a warranty that there are no other transaction-related payments.

### 6. DD-006 export and privacy incident (~1,240 records)
**Why it matters:** The Seller calls it "preliminary" and "not expected to be material." Its own disclosure (DL item 6) says the following are all unknown:
- whether an unauthorised person accessed the file;
- the exact scope of the data involved;
- whether notification is required.

Under the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme in the *Privacy Act 1988* (Cth), an entity that suspects an eligible data breach must complete a reasonable assessment, ordinarily within **30 days** (s 26WH). If the incident predates 22 September 2026, that window may already have closed by today, 5 November 2026. **Please confirm the incident date.** Exposure could include:
- OAIC investigation and civil penalties;
- remediation and notification costs;
- individual complaints;
- potentially claims under the new statutory privacy tort.

Because the general disclosure and Buyer-knowledge clauses would make this a known, excluded matter, only a specific indemnity will protect the Buyer.

**Push back:**
- **Pre-Completion covenants:**
  - complete a forensic investigation, with the scope agreed with the Buyer;
  - complete the NDB assessment;
  - make any required notifications;
  - give the Buyer full information and consultation rights.
- **Specific indemnity** for all Losses arising from the incident, **outside the cap, de minimis, basket and general time limit**, with a tail of at least 3 years. Covered losses should include investigation, notification and remediation costs, third-party claims, and regulator costs to the extent lawfully indemnifiable. Note that indemnities for civil penalties may be unenforceable on public policy grounds, so seek a price reserve as backup.
- Add a warranty that there are no other incidents and no OAIC correspondence.
- Consider a retention sized to the risk.

### 7. Ironquay IP: indemnity limited to the SOW3 payment (cl 11.1)
**Why it matters:** Under DD-004 cl 7.3, ownership of the SOW3 Project Materials transfers only on cleared payment of **every** SOW3 fee. DD-010 shows AUD 180k open. The Seller notes this is not bank verification, and DL item 4 confirms there is no receipt and no confirmatory assignment. The risk is therefore more than AUD 180k: **the Company may not own IP that its product relies on.** An indemnity capped at the fee does not cover:
- infringement claims;
- injunctions;
- rework;
- loss of customers.

**Push back:**
- Make it a **Completion deliverable or CP**: evidence of payment in full of all SOW3 fees, paid by the Seller or deducted from the Price, plus a **confirmatory deed of assignment** from Ironquay, including moral rights consents.
- Broaden the indemnity to **all Losses arising from any failure of the Company to own or have unencumbered rights to the SOW3 Project Materials**, outside the cap and thresholds.
- Clarify what each SOW3 fee covers. The AUD 180k may not be the only unpaid amount.

### 8. Sandbar supplier renewals (3 × AUD 110k = AUD 330k)
**Why it matters:** The Seller calls them ordinary course. Its own disclosure says they are "related" and should be "read together for timing/scope," and it does not say whether they are unavoidable, terminable or accrued. Splitting one AUD 330k commitment into three AUD 110k pieces is a red flag. It may be designed to stay below a material-contract or conduct-of-business threshold. "Related supplier" could also indicate a **Seller-related party**.

**Push back:**
- Ask for the documents, whether Sandbar is related to Harbourglass, the renewal dates and the termination rights.
- Aggregate related contracts when testing any threshold in the conduct-of-business covenant and the warranties.
- If the renewals are not genuinely ordinary course, or Sandbar is a related party, treat the AUD 330k as **leakage or Indebtedness**. Otherwise require that they be terminable without penalty.
- Renewals in the interim period should require Buyer consent.

### 9. General disclosure (DL 1.1–1.2, Schedule 7)
**Why it matters:** Disclosing "every fact, matter and circumstance" in the data room, the Accounts, statutory registers and public records pushes the diligence burden entirely onto the Buyer.

**Push back:**
- Warranties should be qualified **only by matters Fairly Disclosed**: disclosed with sufficient detail for a reasonable buyer to identify the nature, scope and quantum of the matter. Disclosure should be **against specific warranties**.
- Data room disclosure should be limited to an **agreed, indexed copy** delivered on USB to the Buyer, if accepted at all, and still subject to the fair-disclosure standard.
- There should be **no disclosure against Fundamental Warranties, Tax Warranties or any indemnity.**
- DL 1.4 (non-admission) is acceptable, provided it cannot be used to argue that a matter was not "disclosed" for indemnity purposes.

### 10. Buyer knowledge / anti-sandbagging (cl 8.3)
**Why it matters:** This clause excludes claims for anything known to the Buyer **or its advisers**, or "discoverable" from the data room or public records. That is constructive knowledge, and it would cover almost every claim. It also creates disputes about what the Buyer's advisers knew.

**Push back:**
- Delete it, and replace it with an express statement that the Buyer's rights are **not affected by any knowledge or investigation**, other than matters Fairly Disclosed in the Disclosure Letter.
- Fallback: limit it to the **actual knowledge** of a short list of named Buyer individuals, as at signing, of a matter they knew constituted a breach. Exclude advisers and constructive knowledge.

### 11. Cap and thresholds (cl 12.1–12.2)
**Assessment:**
- The **20% cap (AUD 4.8m)** is within range for general warranties. Accept it, or push to 25–30%, only if the issues above are dealt with through specific indemnities and price mechanics.
- The **basket of AUD 250k (~1.04%) is a deductible** ("only the excess" is recoverable). This is Seller-friendly.

**Push back:**
- Ask for a **tipping basket**: once the threshold is reached, the Buyer recovers from the first dollar. Ask for the threshold at around **0.5% (AUD 120k)**.
- Reduce the **de minimis to around AUD 10k–15k** and aggregate related claims for the de minimis test.
- Neither threshold should apply to Fundamental Warranties, Tax, indemnities, leakage or fraud.

### 12. Time limits (cl 12.3/13)
**Push back:**
- **General warranties:** 18 months is acceptable but short. Ask for **24 months** to cover two audit cycles.
- **Tax:** **at least 5–7 years.** This tracks ATO amendment periods (generally 4 years for companies) plus a buffer. There should be no time limit for fraud or evasion.
- **Fundamental warranties:** see issue 4.
- **Indemnities:** each needs its own claim period, for example the incident indemnity and Ironquay at a minimum of 3 years.
- Claims notified in time should not be time-barred by a short window for issuing proceedings. Allow at least 6–9 months after notification.

### 13. Tax and IP "settled under the general regime"
**Push back:**
- Require a **separate tax indemnity** for pre-Completion taxes, including payroll tax on the bonuses. It should be capped at 100% of the Price, sit outside the thresholds and run for 7 years, with Buyer conduct of tax disputes.
- **IP warranties** should be treated as at least "enhanced" for a SaaS target. Consider a higher cap of 30–50% given the Ironquay issue.

### 14. Lower-risk items: lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009)
- **Lease:** DL item 7 describes a notification obligation only. Require the Seller to give the notice in accordance with the lease before or at Completion, and to warrant that no landlord consent is required.
- **Mossvale:** DL item 9 refers to an assignment restriction only. Confirm by our own review that the contract has no change-of-control or deemed-assignment wording. Add a warranty to that effect.

### 15. Security for claims
Harbourglass Ventures appears to be an investment vehicle that may distribute proceeds after Completion. Seek one or more of the following:
- a **retention or escrow** of, say, 10–15% of the Price for 18–24 months, plus specific amounts for the incident and Bluefen;
- a **parent or fund guarantee**;
- a covenant restricting distributions.

Alternatively, consider **W&I insurance**. Note that W&I would not cover these known, disclosed issues, which reinforces the need for specific indemnities and price adjustments.

---

## Summary of recommendations

1. **Do not accept the "FINAL" framing.** Confirm internally whether anything was conceded at principal level. Otherwise all points are open.
2. **Price and funds flow:** Deduct the following from the Price at Completion as Indebtedness or Transaction Costs:
   - the Riverlark payout of ~AUD 3.2m, with a payoff letter, deed of release and PPSR discharges delivered at Completion;
   - the DD-005 bonuses of AUD 420k plus all on-costs;
   - any unpaid Ironquay SOW3 fees;
   - the Sandbar renewals of AUD 330k if they are not genuinely ordinary course or Sandbar is a related party.
3. **Conditions:** Strengthen the Bluefen CP to require unconditional consent (or consent on Buyer-acceptable terms) with all cl 11.3 conditions satisfied, Buyer-only waiver, a long stop and a walk right. Make the Ironquay payment and confirmatory assignment a Completion deliverable.
4. **Specific indemnities, outside the cap and thresholds:**
   - the DD-006 incident, supported by pre-Completion investigation and NDB covenants;
   - Ironquay IP ownership, broadened beyond the fee;
   - bonuses and on-costs;
   - Riverlark;
   - pre-Completion tax.
5. **Liability architecture:**
   - limitations apply only to general Warranty Claims;
   - fraud carve-out throughout;
   - Fundamental and Tax Warranties capped at 100% of the Price with long tails (title 7 years or more and execute as a deed; tax 5–7 years);
   - general cap 20% or higher;
   - tipping basket at ~0.5% and de minimis at ~AUD 10k–15k;
   - general warranty claim period of 24 months.
6. **Disclosure and knowledge:** Replace general disclosure with a fair, specific-disclosure standard, with no disclosure against Fundamental Warranties, Tax or indemnities. Delete cl 8.3 or limit it to the actual knowledge of named individuals.
7. **Security:** Seek a retention or escrow and/or a parent guarantee.
8. **Our own diligence actions:**
   - ASIC and PPSR searches;
   - review of the constitution and shareholder agreements;
   - confirm the DD-006 incident date and NDB timeline status;
   - obtain the Sandbar documents and check for related-party status;
   - check Mossvale and the lease for change-of-control wording;
   - verify the Ironquay payment status directly.

*Note: The statutory references (Privacy Act NDB timing, Limitation Act periods, ATO amendment periods, payroll tax) are stated at a general level. A supervising NSW practitioner should confirm them against current law and the actual SPA clause text before the mark-up goes out.*

### 4. Fundamental (title and capacity) warranties capped and time-limited like general warranties
**Why it matters:** "Administrative simplicity" is not a commercial justification. If title fails, the Buyer has lost the whole AUD 24m, not 20% of it. DL item 10 also relies solely on the company's own register (DD-012) and expressly says the Buyer has not verified it.

**Push back:**
- Title and capacity warranties should be **capped at 100% of the Price**, with no de minimis or basket.
- The claim period should be at least **7 years**, or the statutory limitation period. In NSW that is 6 years for simple contract and 12 years for a deed under the *Limitation Act 1969*. Execute the SPA as a deed if you want the longer period.
- Warranties should cover:
  - no encumbrances over the shares;
  - no options, convertibles, rights to issue or SAFEs;
  - shares fully paid;
  - the register is complete and accurate.
- **Our own steps:** obtain an ASIC company extract and historical search, and run PPSR searches against the Seller and the Company. Review the constitution and any shareholders' agreement for pre-emption rights. At Completion, require signed transfers, share certificates and waivers of pre-emption rights.

### 5. Completion bonuses (AUD 420k, DD-005) omitted from the funds flow
**Why it matters:** The Seller calls these "a matter for the Seller." Legally, however, the **employer company** owes them, so after Completion they become the Buyer's liability. They are triggered by the sale, so they are a transaction cost. DL item 5 also flags that the on-costs are unaddressed:
- PAYG withholding;
- superannuation guarantee, if the bonuses are ordinary time earnings;
- NSW payroll tax;
- workers compensation.

**Push back:**
- Treat the bonuses and **all associated on-costs** as **Indebtedness or Transaction Costs deducted from the Price**, or paid through payroll at Completion out of Seller funds.
- Add a specific indemnity outside the cap and thresholds.
- The continued-employment conditions mean some amounts may fall due after Completion. The Seller should still bear them. Alternatively, the parties could agree that any forfeited amount reverts to the Seller.
- Require the full bonus schedule (recipients, amounts, triggers) and a warranty that there are no other transaction-related payments.

### 6. DD-006 export and privacy incident (~1,240 records)
**Why it matters:** The Seller calls it "preliminary" and "not expected to be material." Its own disclosure (DL item 6) says the following are all unknown:
- whether an unauthorised person accessed the file;
- the exact scope of the data involved;
- whether notification is required.

Under the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme in the *Privacy Act 1988* (Cth), an entity that suspects an eligible data breach must complete a reasonable assessment, ordinarily within **30 days** (s 26WH). If the incident predates 22 September 2026, that window may already have closed by today, 5 November 2026. **Please confirm the incident date.** Exposure could include:
- OAIC investigation and civil penalties;
- remediation and notification costs;
- individual complaints;
- potentially claims under the new statutory privacy tort.

Because the general disclosure and Buyer-knowledge clauses would make this a known, excluded matter, only a specific indemnity will protect the Buyer.

**Push back:**
- **Pre-Completion covenants:**
  - complete a forensic investigation, with the scope agreed with the Buyer;
  - complete the NDB assessment;
  - make any required notifications;
  - give the Buyer full information and consultation rights.
- **Specific indemnity** for all Losses arising from the incident, **outside the cap, de minimis, basket and general time limit**, with a tail of at least 3 years. Covered losses should include investigation, notification and remediation costs, third-party claims, and regulator costs to the extent lawfully indemnifiable. Note that indemnities for civil penalties may be unenforceable on public policy grounds, so seek a price reserve as backup.
- Add a warranty that there are no other incidents and no OAIC correspondence.
- Consider a retention sized to the risk.

### 7. Ironquay IP: indemnity limited to the SOW3 payment (cl 11.1)
**Why it matters:** Under DD-004 cl 7.3, ownership of the SOW3 Project Materials transfers only on cleared payment of **every** SOW3 fee. DD-010 shows AUD 180k open. The Seller notes this is not bank verification, and DL item 4 confirms there is no receipt and no confirmatory assignment. The risk is therefore more than AUD 180k: **the Company may not own IP that its product relies on.** An indemnity capped at the fee does not cover:
- infringement claims;
- injunctions;
- rework;
- loss of customers.

**Push back:**
- Make it a **Completion deliverable or CP**: evidence of payment in full of all SOW3 fees, paid by the Seller or deducted from the Price, plus a **confirmatory deed of assignment** from Ironquay, including moral rights consents.
- Broaden the indemnity to **all Losses arising from any failure of the Company to own or have unencumbered rights to the SOW3 Project Materials**, outside the cap and thresholds.
- Clarify what each SOW3 fee covers. The AUD 180k may not be the only unpaid amount.

### 8. Sandbar supplier renewals (3 × AUD 110k = AUD 330k)
**Why it matters:** The Seller calls them ordinary course. Its own disclosure says they are "related" and should be "read together for timing/scope," and it does not say whether they are unavoidable, terminable or accrued. Splitting one AUD 330k commitment into three AUD 110k pieces is a red flag. It may be designed to stay below a material-contract or conduct-of-business threshold. "Related supplier" could also indicate a **Seller-related party**.

**Push back:**
- Ask for the documents, whether Sandbar is related to Harbourglass, the renewal dates and the termination rights.
- Aggregate related contracts when testing any threshold in the conduct-of-business covenant and the warranties.
- If the renewals are not genuinely ordinary course, or Sandbar is a related party, treat the AUD 330k as **leakage or Indebtedness**. Otherwise require that they be terminable without penalty.
- Renewals in the interim period should require Buyer consent.

### 9. General disclosure (DL 1.1–1.2, Schedule 7)
**Why it matters:** Disclosing "every fact, matter and circumstance" in the data room, the Accounts, statutory registers and public records pushes the diligence burden entirely onto the Buyer.

**Push back:**
- Warranties should be qualified **only by matters Fairly Disclosed**: disclosed with sufficient detail for a reasonable buyer to identify the nature, scope and quantum of the matter. Disclosure should be **against specific warranties**.
- Data room disclosure should be limited to an **agreed, indexed copy** delivered on USB to the Buyer, if accepted at all, and still subject to the fair-disclosure standard.
- There should be **no disclosure against Fundamental Warranties, Tax Warranties or any indemnity.**
- DL 1.4 (non-admission) is acceptable, provided it cannot be used to argue that a matter was not "disclosed" for indemnity purposes.

### 10. Buyer knowledge / anti-sandbagging (cl 8.3)
**Why it matters:** This clause excludes claims for anything known to the Buyer **or its advisers**, or "discoverable" from the data room or public records. That is constructive knowledge, and it would cover almost every claim. It also creates disputes about what the Buyer's advisers knew.

**Push back:**
- Delete it, and replace it with an express statement that the Buyer's rights are **not affected by any knowledge or investigation**, other than matters Fairly Disclosed in the Disclosure Letter.
- Fallback: limit it to the **actual knowledge** of a short list of named Buyer individuals, as at signing, of a matter they knew constituted a breach. Exclude advisers and constructive knowledge.

### 11. Cap and thresholds (cl 12.1–12.2)
**Assessment:**
- The **20% cap (AUD 4.8m)** is within range for general warranties. Accept it, or push to 25–30%, only if the issues above are dealt with through specific indemnities and price mechanics.
- The **basket of AUD 250k (~1.04%) is a deductible** ("only the excess" is recoverable). This is Seller-friendly.

**Push back:**
- Ask for a **tipping basket**: once the threshold is reached, the Buyer recovers from the first dollar. Ask for the threshold at around **0.5% (AUD 120k)**.
- Reduce the **de minimis to around AUD 10k–15k** and aggregate related claims for the de minimis test.
- Neither threshold should apply to Fundamental Warranties, Tax, indemnities, leakage or fraud.

### 12. Time limits (cl 12.3/13)
**Push back:**
- **General warranties:** 18 months is acceptable but short. Ask for **24 months** to cover two audit cycles.
- **Tax:** **at least 5–7 years.** This tracks ATO amendment periods (generally 4 years for companies) plus a buffer. There should be no time limit for fraud or evasion.
- **Fundamental warranties:** see issue 4.
- **Indemnities:** each needs its own claim period, for example the incident indemnity and Ironquay at a minimum of 3 years.
- Claims notified in time should not be time-barred by a short window for issuing proceedings. Allow at least 6–9 months after notification.

### 13. Tax and IP "settled under the general regime"
**Push back:**
- Require a **separate tax indemnity** for pre-Completion taxes, including payroll tax on the bonuses. It should be capped at 100% of the Price, sit outside the thresholds and run for 7 years, with Buyer conduct of tax disputes.
- **IP warranties** should be treated as at least "enhanced" for a SaaS target. Consider a higher cap of 30–50% given the Ironquay issue.

### 14. Lower-risk items: lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009)
- **Lease:** DL item 7 describes a notification obligation only. Require the Seller to give the notice in accordance with the lease before or at Completion, and to warrant that no landlord consent is required.
- **Mossvale:** DL item 9 refers to an assignment restriction only. Confirm by our own review that the contract has no change-of-control or deemed-assignment wording. Add a warranty to that effect.

### 15. Security for claims
Harbourglass Ventures appears to be an investment vehicle that may distribute proceeds after Completion. Seek one or more of the following:
- a **retention or escrow** of, say, 10–15% of the Price for 18–24 months, plus specific amounts for the incident and Bluefen;
- a **parent or fund guarantee**;
- a covenant restricting distributions.

Alternatively, consider **W&I insurance**. Note that W&I would not cover these known, disclosed issues, which reinforces the need for specific indemnities and price adjustments.

---

## Summary of recommendations

1. **Do not accept the "FINAL" framing.** Confirm internally whether anything was conceded at principal level. Otherwise all points are open.
2. **Price and funds flow:** Deduct the following from the Price at Completion as Indebtedness or Transaction Costs:
   - the Riverlark payout of ~AUD 3.2m, with a payoff letter, deed of release and PPSR discharges delivered at Completion;
   - the DD-005 bonuses of AUD 420k plus all on-costs;
   - any unpaid Ironquay SOW3 fees;
   - the Sandbar renewals of AUD 330k if they are not genuinely ordinary course or Sandbar is a related party.
3. **Conditions:** Strengthen the Bluefen CP to require unconditional consent (or consent on Buyer-acceptable terms) with all cl 11.3 conditions satisfied, Buyer-only waiver, a long stop and a walk right. Make the Ironquay payment and confirmatory assignment a Completion deliverable.
4. **Specific indemnities, outside the cap and thresholds:**
   - the DD-006 incident, supported by pre-Completion investigation and NDB covenants;
   - Ironquay IP ownership, broadened beyond the fee;
   - bonuses and on-costs;
   - Riverlark;
   - pre-Completion tax.
5. **Liability architecture:**
   - limitations apply only to general Warranty Claims;
   - fraud carve-out throughout;
   - Fundamental and Tax Warranties capped at 100% of the Price with long tails (title 7 years or more and execute as a deed; tax 5–7 years);
   - general cap 20% or higher;
   - tipping basket at ~0.5% and de minimis at ~AUD 10k–15k;
   - general warranty claim period of 24 months.
6. **Disclosure and knowledge:** Replace general disclosure with a fair, specific-disclosure standard, with no disclosure against Fundamental Warranties, Tax or indemnities. Delete cl 8.3 or limit it to the actual knowledge of named individuals.
7. **Security:** Seek a retention or escrow and/or a parent guarantee.
8. **Our own diligence actions:**
   - ASIC and PPSR searches;
   - review of the constitution and shareholder agreements;
   - confirm the DD-006 incident date and NDB timeline status;
   - obtain the Sandbar documents and check for related-party status;
   - check Mossvale and the lease for change-of-control wording;
   - verify the Ironquay payment status directly.

*Note: The statutory references (Privacy Act NDB timing, Limitation Act periods, ATO amendment periods, payroll tax) are stated at a general level. A supervising NSW practitioner should confirm them against current law and the actual SPA clause text before the mark-up goes out.*
